# Quick intro

This version asks a narrower question than the previous capacity-based model:

> **Can persistent differences in the propensity to engage executive function (EF) emerge through experience, without assuming stable differences in EF capacity?**

The model is intentionally minimal. We start from established theories of cognitive-control allocation and learning, then ask what happens when the same mechanisms are iterated over a developmental time horizon.

The core distinction is:

- **Fast process:** a moment-to-moment decision about whether EF is worth engaging.
- **Slow processes:** learned expectations about
  - the value of engaging EF, and
  - how effortful engaging EF feels.

This version deliberately removes from the core model:

- a separate EF capacity state $K(t)$;
- an explicit maturation term;
- an age-dependent growth-opportunity function;
- a built-in sensitive period;
- individual differences in starting capacity.

The first goal is to see what **experience-dependent control learning alone** can and cannot generate.

The key phenomena we want to test are:

1. **Developmental improvement:** average EF engagement increases over accumulated experience.
2. **Emerging individual differences:** initially similar children become more different over time.
3. **Persistent individual differences:** relative differences persist across developmental periods rather than simply reflecting momentary noise.
4. **Transient contextual fluctuations:** temporary stress can lower engagement and engagement can recover.
5. **Intervention timing:** test whether early support has stronger later consequences *without* assuming an age-dependent growth window.

::: {.callout-important}
## The logic of this version

The aim is **not** to force all five phenomena to appear.

If a minimal model fails to generate a phenomenon, that is theoretically informative. We then add one mechanism at a time and ask what additional assumption is actually required.
:::

# Relationship to established control models

## Expected Value of Control (EVC): the fast decision

The Expected Value of Control framework defines the value of a candidate control signal as its expected payoff minus the cost of exerting that control:

$$
\mathrm{EVC}(\text{signal},\text{state})
=
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Payoff}\mid \text{signal},\text{state}]
-
\mathrm{Cost}(\text{signal}).
$$

The expected payoff depends on possible outcomes, their probabilities, and their values.

Reference: [Shenhav, Botvinick, & Cohen (2013), *The Expected Value of Control*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3767969/).

Our model is a deliberately simplified binary version of this idea. At each episode, the agent can either:

$$
A_t=1 \quad \text{engage EF},
$$

or

$$
A_t=0 \quad \text{do not engage EF}.
$$

Rather than solving over a continuous range of control signals, we reduce the problem to a binary choice: engage EF or do not engage EF. We track a single net value for engaging EF relative to not engaging, which is treated as the baseline.

## Learned Value of Control (LVOC): learning from experience

The Learned Value of Control model proposes that agents can learn to predict the value of candidate control signals from previous experience instead of recomputing the full control problem from scratch each time.

Reference: [Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, & Griffiths (2018), *Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control*](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006043).

The full LVOC model uses a richer feature-based approximation to the value of control. We do **not** reproduce that full model here. Instead, we borrow its core principle:

> experienced outcomes update the expected value assigned to future control.

Our $V_t$ should therefore be interpreted as a simplified learned expected payoff of engaging EF, not as an implementation of the full LVOC algorithm.

## Learning Expected Value of Control (LEVC): practice changes the future agent

LEVC extends EVC to situations in which experience changes what the agent will be able to do later. In the original LEVC model, task-specific **automaticity** increases with experience. Higher automaticity means that the same level of performance can be achieved with less cognitive control.

References:

- [Masís, Musslick, & Cohen (2021), *The Value of Learning and Cognitive Control Allocation*](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/7w0223v0)
- [Masís Obando, Musslick, & Cohen (2025), *Learning expectations shape cognitive control allocation*](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2416720122)

In the 2021 formulation, automaticity in a learnable task is assumed to increase with the number of times that task has been practiced:

$$
\mathrm{automaticity}_{L}
=
\alpha_L n_{\mathrm{trials},L}
+
\mathrm{automaticity}_{0,L}.
$$

Automaticity then changes the relationship between control intensity and accuracy: greater automaticity allows equal accuracy with less control.

This is closely related to the developmental mechanism we need, but it also creates an important distinction:

$$
\text{control engagement}
\neq
\text{observed EF performance}.
$$

A child may become better at a practiced task while requiring less control to perform it.

The practice-related cost rule below can also be rewritten in a more intuitive way. Instead of tracking only how subjective effort cost decreases, we can equivalently track how much **practice-related improvement** has accumulated. In that representation, engaging EF increases a bounded practice state, with progressively smaller gains as the child approaches the maximum amount of practice-related improvement. This is not a new mechanism; it is simply another way of writing the same cost dynamics.

This is similar in spirit to LEVC, where practice increases task-specific automaticity, but our model does not explicitly model automaticity or task performance. We therefore interpret the corresponding state more generally as accumulated practice or learned efficiency rather than claiming that it is automaticity itself.

## Empirical precedent for learned control allocation

Bustamante et al. used a Stroop task in which participants learned through reward which stimulus features predicted that using the more control-demanding response would pay off. When those features later appeared in new combinations, participants carried that learning over and sometimes chose the more effortful control response even when it was no longer the rewarded option.

Reference: [Bustamante, Lieder, Musslick, Shenhav, & Cohen (2021), *Learning to Overexert Cognitive Control in a Stroop Task*](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13415-020-00845-x).

This provides evidence that the **decision to engage cognitive control** can be shaped by past experience and generalize to later situations. It does not directly test our proposed practice-to-lower-effort mechanism.

# What is new here?

EVC, LVOC, and LEVC focus primarily on how control is allocated and learned within task environments.

Our question is different:

> **What happens to a population when experience-dependent control learning is iterated over a much longer developmental horizon?**

In particular:

> Can small differences in early experience produce later, persistent differences in EF engagement even when children begin with the same model parameters and no capacity differences?

# Core model

At each episode, the child implicitly evaluates:

> **Is engaging EF worth it right now?**

That decision depends on two slowly changing, experience-dependent quantities:

- $V(t)$: how much engaging EF is expected to pay off;
- $C(t)$: how effortful engaging EF currently feels.

Temporary context, such as acute stress, can also make engagement less attractive in the moment. Together, these determine the **net value of engaging EF**, which sets the child's likelihood of engaging, $\pi(t)$. The actual engagement decision, $A(t)$, is probabilistic.

What happens next feeds back into future decisions. The reward environment determines how often engagement actually pays off, and experienced outcomes update $V(t)$. At the same time, engaging EF provides practice, which can gradually make future engagement easier by lowering $C(t)$.

Thus, the model contains two experience-dependent feedback pathways:

$$
\text{engage EF}
\rightarrow
\text{learn whether it pays off}
\rightarrow
V(t)
\rightarrow
\text{future engagement},
$$

and

$$
\text{engage EF}
\rightarrow
\text{practice / learned efficiency}
\rightarrow
C(t)\downarrow
\rightarrow
\text{future engagement}.
$$

**Colors indicate the role of each component:** orange = slow experience-dependent states; green = momentary decision value; blue = fast engagement process; purple = experienced outcome; dashed gray = external context or environment.

The model separates a **likelihood** from an **actual decision**:

$$
\pi_t = \text{probability of engaging EF}
$$

and

$$
A_t \in \{0,1\} = \text{whether EF is actually engaged on that episode}.
$$

Learning occurs from the actual experience $A_t$, not from a fractional expected engagement value. This distinction matters for the developmental question because two initially identical children can receive different sequences of engagement and reward outcomes simply by chance.

## 1. Fast control decision

For child $i$ at episode $t$, define the **net value of engaging EF** as

$$
D_{i,t}
=
V_{i,t}
-
C_{i,t}
-
X_{i,t},
$$

where:

- $V_{i,t}$ is the learned expected payoff of engaging EF;
- $C_{i,t}$ is the effective subjective effort cost;
- $X_{i,t}$ is a temporary contextual cost, such as acute stress.

Thus, larger $D_{i,t}$ means that engaging EF currently looks more worthwhile; smaller $D_{i,t}$ means that the expected payoff is less favorable relative to effort and context.

We map this net value onto a probability of engagement:

$$
\pi_{i,t}
=
\sigma\left(
\frac{D_{i,t}}{\tau}
\right),
$$

where

$$
\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.
$$

Actual engagement is probabilistic:

$$
A_{i,t}
\sim
\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{i,t}).
$$

The temperature parameter $\tau$ controls how sharply differences in net value translate into behavior.

::: {.callout-note}
## Relation to the original EVC framework

The model keeps the basic EVC idea that control is more likely to be engaged when its expected benefits outweigh its costs, but simplifies the decision to two options: **engage EF** or **do not engage EF**. We explicitly model the net value of engaging EF and treat not engaging as the baseline.

A richer extension could assign and learn separate values for both options.
:::

## 2. Experienced reward

Both the engagement decision and the payoff outcome are binary. The engagement variable is

$$
A_{i,t}\in\{0,1\},
$$

and the payoff indicator is

$$
Y_{i,t}
\sim
\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{i,t}),
$$

where $Y_{i,t}=1$ means that engaging EF pays off on that episode and $Y_{i,t}=0$ means that it does not. The experienced reward is

$$
R_{i,t}
=
A_{i,t}Y_{i,t}r,
$$

where $r>0$ is the magnitude of the payoff. Therefore, the child receives $r$ only when EF is both engaged ($A_{i,t}=1$) and rewarded ($Y_{i,t}=1$); otherwise the experienced reward is $0$.

If EF is not engaged, $V_{i,t}$ is not updated. In this minimal model, the child learns about the payoff of engaging EF only from occasions on which EF is actually engaged. The model therefore does not include counterfactual learning about what would have happened had the child engaged EF, or learning from observing others.

## 3. Learned expected payoff

We use a standard **delta-learning rule**, in which an expectation is updated according to the prediction error between what was experienced and what was expected:

$$
V_{i,t+1}
=
V_{i,t}
+
\alpha_V A_{i,t}
\left(
R_{i,t}-V_{i,t}
\right).
$$

Here, $R_{i,t}-V_{i,t}$ is the prediction error. Thus:

- rewarded engagement can increase learned value;
- unrewarded engagement can decrease learned value;
- if EF is not engaged, $A_{i,t}=0$ and $V_{i,t+1}=V_{i,t}$.

This learning rule is inspired by LVOC's idea that the value of cognitive control can be learned from experience. However, we use a much simpler delta-learning rule that tracks only the expected payoff of engaging EF, rather than LVOC's richer feature-based representation of different control options.

## 4. Practice-dependent effective effort cost

The cost-side hypothesis is that **actually engaging EF creates practice**, and practice can make the same kind of control easier to deploy later. Non-engagement is therefore a lost practice opportunity rather than an event that directly makes EF harder.

We start with the following reduced-form equation:

$$
C_{i,t+1}
=
C_{i,t}
-
\alpha_C A_{i,t}
\left(
C_{i,t}-C_{\min}
\right).
$$

Thus:

- engaging EF moves effective subjective cost toward a lower bound $C_{\min}$;
- not engaging EF does not directly increase cost;
- the size of the practice effect shrinks as there is less remaining room for improvement.

### The same cost rule can be written as accumulated practice

The equation above tracks how effort cost falls with practice. The same mechanism can be written in a more intuitive way by tracking **how much of the possible practice-related improvement has accumulated**. This is only a change in representation; it does not add another process to the model.

Define a practice/learned-efficiency state as the proportion of the possible practice-related cost reduction that has already occurred:

$$
L_{i,t}
=
\frac{C_0-C_{i,t}}{C_0-C_{\min}}.
$$

Then $L=0$ corresponds to the initial effort level and $L=1$ corresponds to the practice limit $C_{\min}$.

Starting from

$$
C_{i,t+1}-C_{\min}
=
(C_{i,t}-C_{\min})
(1-\alpha_C A_{i,t}),
$$

the same dynamics can be written as

$$
\boxed{
L_{i,t+1}
=
L_{i,t}
+
\alpha_C A_{i,t}(1-L_{i,t})
}
$$

with

$$
C_{i,t}
=
C_{\min}
+
(C_0-C_{\min})(1-L_{i,t}).
$$

So the same practice mechanism can be written in two mathematically equivalent ways:

$$
\text{practice}
\rightarrow
C_t\downarrow
$$

or, using the alternative practice state $L_t$,

$$
\text{practice}
\rightarrow
L_t\uparrow.
$$

These are **not two separate psychological processes**. $L_t$ is calculated directly from $C_t$, so knowing one determines the other. The $L_t$ representation is useful because it makes the practice interpretation intuitive: repeated engagement accumulates practice, but the amount of further improvement becomes smaller as $L_t$ approaches 1.

This is close in spirit to LEVC, which proposes that task experience can increase automaticity and thereby reduce the amount of control needed for successful performance. Our model is simpler in two ways:

1. We use a **bounded, saturating** practice process because the model is run over a long developmental horizon.
2. We do not separately model automaticity, control intensity, and task accuracy. The current model asks only whether EF is engaged, so practice-related improvement is represented through the single effort-cost state $C_t$.

For the current engagement model, we therefore keep $C_t$ as the primary state and treat $L_t$ only as an alternative way of describing the same practice-related change. A separate automaticity or skill state would become useful if we later wanted to model **how well the child performs an EF task**, in addition to whether the child engages EF.

::: {.callout-important}
## How practice is represented in the current model

Reward experience and practice affect two different learned quantities.

- $V_t$ represents **how worthwhile engaging EF is expected to be**. It is updated from experienced reward outcomes.
- $C_t$ represents **how effortful engaging EF currently is**. It is not learned from an explicit observation of how effortful the previous attempt felt. Instead, the model assumes that each occasion of EF engagement provides practice, which gradually lowers $C_t$ toward $C_{\min}$.

Thus, reward experience changes whether EF seems **worthwhile**, whereas practice changes how **effortful** EF feels.
:::

## How current engagement shapes future engagement

Current engagement can affect later engagement through two experience-dependent pathways.

**1. Practice pathway**

When EF is engaged, the child gets practice. Repeated practice gradually lowers the effective effort cost of engaging EF, which makes future engagement more likely:

$$
A_t=1
\rightarrow
\text{practice}
\rightarrow
C_{t+1}\downarrow
\rightarrow
\pi_{t+1}\uparrow.
$$

This is a reinforcing pathway: engaging EF now can make EF easier to engage later. A higher $\pi_{t+1}$ makes later engagement more likely, although the actual decision remains probabilistic.

**2. Value-learning pathway**

Engaging EF also gives the child an opportunity to observe whether doing so pays off:

$$
A_t=1
\rightarrow
\text{experienced reward }R_t
\rightarrow
V_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\pi_{t+1}.
$$

If the payoff is better than expected, $V_t$ increases and future engagement becomes more likely. If the payoff is worse than expected, $V_t$ decreases and future engagement becomes less likely. Unlike the practice pathway, this pathway is therefore not always reinforcing in the positive direction.

Together, the two pathways capture different consequences of experience: **practice changes how effortful EF feels, while reward outcomes change how worthwhile EF seems**. Both can feed back into the likelihood of engaging EF on later occasions.

# Why differentiation grows and then weakens

The simulations are easier to interpret if we first combine learned payoff and learned effort cost into one quantity. Ignoring temporary context for the moment, define

$$
D_t=V_t-C_t.
$$

$D_t$ is the **net value of engaging EF** before the logistic decision rule is applied:

$$
\pi_t
=
\sigma\left(
\frac{D_t}{\tau}
\right).
$$

Suppose for now that the reward environment is stable, so the probability that EF engagement pays off remains constant at $p$. If the reward magnitude is $r$, then $pr$ is the **average payoff available when EF is engaged**. It is not a hard upper bound on $V_t$; rather, it is the long-run value toward which reward learning tends on average in a stable environment.

We can then ask how much each learned quantity is expected to change from one episode to the next. Because engagement decisions and reward outcomes are probabilistic, these equations describe the **average expected change**, not what must happen on every individual episode:

$$
\mathbb{E}[V_{t+1}-V_t\mid V_t,C_t]
=
\alpha_V\pi_t(pr-V_t)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{E}[C_{t+1}-C_t\mid V_t,C_t]
=
-\alpha_C\pi_t(C_t-C_{\min}).
$$

Since $D_t=V_t-C_t$,

$$
\boxed{
\mathbb{E}[D_{t+1}-D_t\mid V_t,C_t]
=
\pi_t
\underbrace{\left[
\alpha_V(pr-V_t)
+
\alpha_C(C_t-C_{\min})
\right]}_{\text{remaining potential for reward learning and practice}}
}
$$

The two terms inside the brackets have a simple interpretation:

- $pr-V_t$ indicates how far the child's current expected payoff is below the average payoff available in the environment;
- $C_t-C_{\min}$ indicates how much further practice could still reduce the effective effort cost.

Early in development, there may therefore be substantial room for both reward learning and practice-related improvement. A child who happens to have a somewhat higher $D_t$ is more likely to engage EF, and engaging creates more opportunities for both kinds of updating:

$$
D_t\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\pi_t\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\text{more opportunities for reward learning and practice}.
$$

This can amplify chance differences over a developmental period. It does **not** mean that a child who is slightly ahead must keep moving farther ahead forever. As $V_t$ approaches $pr$ and $C_t$ approaches $C_{\min}$, there is progressively less left to learn or improve, so this reinforcing effect becomes weaker.

::: {.callout-note}
## What this does and does not imply

The equation identifies a mechanism through which chance differences in experience can become temporarily self-reinforcing. It does not imply that every parameter setting produces large or permanent individual differences.

How much differentiation appears depends on the learning rates, decision temperature, initial net value, the amount by which practice can still reduce effort cost, and the developmental horizon. We test that dependence explicitly in the replicated parameter analysis below.
:::

## Common long-run regime

The mean deterministic tendencies are toward

$$
V^*=pr
$$

and

$$
C^*=C_{\min}.
$$

The corresponding common mean-control regime is

$$
\pi^*
=
\sigma\left(
\frac{pr-C_{\min}}{\tau}
\right).
$$

This common regime applies when children share the same stable reward environment. If reward probability differs persistently across children, $p_i$, then

$$
V_i^*=p_ir,
\qquad
C_i^*=C_{\min},
$$

and the corresponding long-run mean engagement levels can also differ:

$$
\pi_i^*
=
\sigma\left(
\frac{p_ir-C_{\min}}{\tau}
\right).
$$

So the model distinguishes two sources of developmental differentiation:

- **chance differences in experience under the same environment** can make initially identical children diverge over a developmental horizon;
- **persistent environmental differences** can additionally maintain different long-run mean engagement levels.


Because choices and reward outcomes remain probabilistic with a constant learning rate, individual trajectories need not collapse to a single point. They continue to fluctuate around their relevant long-run mean regime.

The stronger developmental questions are therefore:

1. **Developmental differentiation:** can chance differences in experience cause initially identical children to develop substantial differences in EF engagement over a developmentally relevant period, even when they share the same environment?
2. **Rank persistence:** once children have begun to differ, do those who are relatively high or low in EF engagement tend to retain their relative position over time, or does that ordering eventually disappear?
3. **Environmental stabilization:** can small persistent differences in reward environments stabilize which children remain relatively high or low?

This distinction prevents us from calling developmental-horizon differentiation a set of permanently distinct asymptotic states.

# Model ladder

Rather than fitting one large model, we compare nested versions.

| Model | Fast EVC-like choice | Learned value | Practice lowers cost | Passive cost stabilization |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| M0: EVC only | yes | no | no | no |
| M1: + value learning | yes | yes | no | no |
| M2: + practice-cost feedback | yes | yes | yes | no |
| M3: + cost stabilization | yes | yes | yes | yes |

The core paper should initially focus on M0-M2.

M3 is included as a diagnostic extension because Yuko previously asked whether a baseline cost level / mean-reversion term is actually necessary.

# Simulation setup

## General choices

These are qualitative simulations, not fitted developmental estimates.

- Time in the model represents repeated opportunities to engage EF, rather than literal weeks or years.
- Figures show the literal simulation episode $t$; time is not normalized.
- All agents have identical starting $V_0$ and $C_0$ in the primary analyses.
- All agents have identical learning parameters.
- Chance differences arise from the realized engagement decisions and reward outcomes.
- We later introduce a *very small* between-child difference in reward probability as an environmental heterogeneity test.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Parameter status

The default parameters below are provisional. They are chosen to keep the system away from immediate floor/ceiling behavior so that the qualitative dynamics are visible, not as empirical estimates.
:::

| Quantity | Default | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| $N$ | 800 | Number of simulated children in the default population |
| $T$ | 1500 | Number of developmental episodes |
| $V_0$ | 0.577 | Initial learned expected payoff from engaging EF |
| $C_0$ | 0.987 | Initial effective effort cost of engaging EF |
| $\tau$ | 0.163 | Decision temperature; larger values make engagement less tightly determined by $D_t=V_t-C_t-X_t$ |
| $p$ | 0.591 | Probability that EF engagement pays off in the default environment |
| $r$ | 1.150 | Reward magnitude when engagement pays off |
| $\alpha_V$ | 0.0244 | Value-learning rate |
| $\alpha_C$ | 0.00263 | Practice-related cost-reduction rate |
| $C_{\min}$ | 0.459 | Lower limit on effective effort cost under practice |
| $C_{\mathrm{set}}$ | 0.987 | Baseline cost level used only in optional M3 |
| $\eta_C$ | 0.0008 | Passive cost-stabilization rate used only in optional M3 |

$N$ and $T$ are simulation-design choices rather than psychological parameters. The remaining values specify the provisional default model used for the illustrative simulations.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

# Dependency-free parallel helper.
# macOS/Linux: fork-based parallelism using base R's parallel package.
# Windows: sequential fallback.
parallel_lapply <- function(X, FUN, ..., workers = NULL) {

  if (is.null(workers)) {
    detected <- parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)

    if (is.na(detected) || detected <= 1L) {
      workers <- 1L
    } else {
      # Leave one physical core available for the OS / RStudio.
      workers <- max(1L, detected - 1L)
    }
  }

  if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows" || workers <= 1L) {
    return(lapply(X, FUN, ...))
  }

  parallel::mclapply(
    X,
    FUN,
    ...,
    mc.cores = workers,
    mc.preschedule = TRUE,
    mc.set.seed = TRUE
  )
}
```
