```{r}
  "Later support" = "#D96C4A",
  "Identical environment" = "#4C78A8",
  "Persistent reward differences (SD = .02)" = "#B56576"
)

snapshot_cols <- c(
  "Early" = "#B56576",
  "Middle" = "#6A994E",
  "Late" = "#4E79A7"
)

theme_result <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        size = base_size,
        margin = margin(b = 7)
      ),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(
        size = base_size - 2,
        margin = margin(b = 6)
      ),
      axis.title.y = element_text(
        margin = margin(r = 12)
      ),
      axis.title.x = element_text(
        margin = margin(t = 8)
      ),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.margin = margin(14, 26, 14, 34)
    )
}

```


```{r}
#| label: simulate_population
#| echo: true

simulate_population <- function(
  model = c("evc", "value", "value_cost", "value_cost_stabilized"),

  N = default_pars$N,
  T = default_pars$T,

  V0 = default_pars$V0,
  C0 = default_pars$C0,

  tau = default_pars$tau,

  p_reward = default_pars$p_reward,
  p_reward_sd = 0,
  reward_mag = default_pars$reward_mag,

  alpha_V = default_pars$alpha_V,
  alpha_C = default_pars$alpha_C,
  C_min = default_pars$C_min,

  C_set = default_pars$C_set,
  eta_C = default_pars$eta_C,

  p_reward_shift = NULL,
  extra_cost = NULL,

  record_every = default_pars$record_every,
  seed = 1
) {

  model <- match.arg(model)

  stopifnot(N >= 2, T >= 2, tau > 0)
  stopifnot(alpha_V >= 0, alpha_C >= 0, eta_C >= 0)
  stopifnot(C_min < C0)

  if (is.null(p_reward_shift)) p_reward_shift <- rep(0, T)
  if (is.null(extra_cost)) extra_cost <- rep(0, T)

  stopifnot(length(p_reward_shift) == T)
  stopifnot(length(extra_cost) == T)

  set.seed(seed)

  child_id <- seq_len(N)

  # Primary analyses use p_reward_sd = 0.
  # A later analysis introduces a very small persistent environmental difference.
  p_i <- clip(rnorm(N, mean = p_reward, sd = p_reward_sd))

  V <- rep(V0, N)
  C <- rep(C0, N)

  out <- vector("list", ceiling(T / record_every) + 2)
  k <- 1

  for (tt in seq_len(T)) {

    p_t <- clip(p_i + p_reward_shift[tt])

    decision_value <- V - C - extra_cost[tt]
    pi_engage <- plogis(decision_value / tau)

    # Actual engagement decision.
    A <- as.integer(runif(N) < pi_engage)

    # Potential reward outcome. It only enters learning when A = 1.
    reward_success <- as.integer(runif(N) < p_t)
    reward_observed <- A * reward_success * reward_mag

    if (tt == 1 || tt %% record_every == 0 || tt == T) {
      out[[k]] <- tibble(
        child_id = child_id,
        step = tt,

        p_reward_child = p_i,
        p_reward_used = p_t,
        extra_cost = extra_cost[tt],

        V = V,
        C = C,
        effective_cost = C + extra_cost[tt],

        decision_value = decision_value,
        pi = pi_engage,
        A = A,
        reward = reward_observed
      )

      k <- k + 1
    }

    # M1-M3: learn expected payoff from actual engagement outcomes.
    if (model %in% c("value", "value_cost", "value_cost_stabilized")) {
      V <- V + alpha_V * A * (reward_observed - V)
    }

    # M2-M3: actual engagement gradually lowers subjective effort cost.
    if (model %in% c("value_cost", "value_cost_stabilized")) {
      C <- C - alpha_C * A * (C - C_min)
    }

    # M3 only: passive return toward a baseline cost level.
    # This is tested as an additional mechanism, not assumed in the core model.
    if (model == "value_cost_stabilized") {
      C <- C + eta_C * (C_set - C)
    }

    # Numerical bounds.
    V <- clip(V, lo = 0, hi = reward_mag)
    C <- pmax(C, C_min)
  }

  bind_rows(out[seq_len(k - 1)]) %>%
    mutate(
      model = model,
      model_label = unname(model_labels[model])
    )
}
```


```{r}
#| label: diagnostics_helpers
#| echo: true

population_summary <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    group_by(model_label, step) %>%
    summarize(
      mean_pi = mean(pi),
      sd_pi = sd(pi),
      mean_V = mean(V),
      mean_C = mean(C),
      mean_A = mean(A),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

window_score <- function(df, lo, hi, label) {
  T_end <- max(df$step)
  lo_step <- episode_at_fraction(T_end, lo)
  hi_step <- episode_at_fraction(T_end, hi)

  df %>%
    filter(step >= lo_step, step <= hi_step) %>%
    group_by(child_id) %>%
    summarize(
      score = mean(pi),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(window = label)
}

stability_table <- function(df) {

  scores <- bind_rows(
    window_score(df, 0.20, 0.30, "Early"),
    window_score(df, 0.50, 0.60, "Middle"),
    window_score(df, 0.85, 0.95, "Late")
  ) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = window,
      values_from = score
    )

  tibble(
    comparison = c(
      "Early vs Middle",
      "Middle vs Late",
      "Early vs Late"
    ),
    spearman_rho = suppressWarnings(c(
      cor(scores$Early, scores$Middle, method = "spearman"),
      cor(scores$Middle, scores$Late, method = "spearman"),
      cor(scores$Early, scores$Late, method = "spearman")
    ))
  )
}

development_metrics <- function(df) {

  T_end <- max(df$step)
  early_lo <- episode_at_fraction(T_end, 0.20)
  early_hi <- episode_at_fraction(T_end, 0.30)
  late_lo <- episode_at_fraction(T_end, 0.85)
  late_hi <- episode_at_fraction(T_end, 0.95)

  early <- df %>% filter(step >= early_lo, step <= early_hi)
  late  <- df %>% filter(step >= late_lo, step <= late_hi)

  early_sd <- early %>%
    group_by(step) %>%
    summarize(x = sd(pi), .groups = "drop") %>%
    summarize(x = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    pull(x)

  late_sd <- late %>%
    group_by(step) %>%
    summarize(x = sd(pi), .groups = "drop") %>%
    summarize(x = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    pull(x)

  stab <- stability_table(df)

  tibble(
    early_mean = mean(early$pi),
    late_mean = mean(late$pi),
    delta_mean = late_mean - early_mean,
    early_sd = early_sd,
    late_sd = late_sd,
    sd_gain = late_sd - early_sd,
    rho_middle_late = stab$spearman_rho[stab$comparison == "Middle vs Late"],
    rho_early_late = stab$spearman_rho[stab$comparison == "Early vs Late"]
  )
}

get_snapshot <- function(df, target, label) {
  target_step <- episode_at_fraction(max(df$step), target)

  df %>%
    group_by(child_id) %>%
    slice_min(
      order_by = abs(step - target_step),
      n = 1,
      with_ties = FALSE
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(snapshot = label)
}

# Lightweight simulator for parameter sweeps.
# It computes only the early/middle/late summaries needed by
# development_metrics(), rather than constructing a full trajectory tibble.
simulate_development_metrics_fast <- function(
  N,
  T,
  V0,
  C0,
  tau,
  p_reward,
  reward_mag = default_pars$reward_mag,
  alpha_V,
  alpha_C,
  C_min,
  record_every = 10,
  seed = 1
) {

  set.seed(seed)

  V <- rep(V0, N)
  C <- rep(C0, N)

  early_sum <- 0
  late_sum <- 0
  early_n <- 0L
  late_n <- 0L

  early_sd_sum <- 0
  late_sd_sum <- 0
  early_sd_n <- 0L
  late_sd_n <- 0L

  early_child_sum <- numeric(N)
  middle_child_sum <- numeric(N)
  late_child_sum <- numeric(N)

  early_child_n <- 0L
  middle_child_n <- 0L
  late_child_n <- 0L

  early_lo <- episode_at_fraction(T, 0.20)
  early_hi <- episode_at_fraction(T, 0.30)
  middle_lo <- episode_at_fraction(T, 0.50)
  middle_hi <- episode_at_fraction(T, 0.60)
  late_lo <- episode_at_fraction(T, 0.85)
  late_hi <- episode_at_fraction(T, 0.95)

  for (tt in seq_len(T)) {

    pi_engage <- plogis((V - C) / tau)

    record_this <- (
      tt == 1 ||
      tt %% record_every == 0 ||
      tt == T
    )

    if (record_this) {

      if (tt >= early_lo && tt <= early_hi) {
        early_sum <- early_sum + sum(pi_engage)
        early_n <- early_n + N
        early_sd_sum <- early_sd_sum + sd(pi_engage)
        early_sd_n <- early_sd_n + 1L
        early_child_sum <- early_child_sum + pi_engage
        early_child_n <- early_child_n + 1L
      }

      if (tt >= middle_lo && tt <= middle_hi) {
        middle_child_sum <- middle_child_sum + pi_engage
        middle_child_n <- middle_child_n + 1L
      }

      if (tt >= late_lo && tt <= late_hi) {
        late_sum <- late_sum + sum(pi_engage)
        late_n <- late_n + N
        late_sd_sum <- late_sd_sum + sd(pi_engage)
        late_sd_n <- late_sd_n + 1L
        late_child_sum <- late_child_sum + pi_engage
        late_child_n <- late_child_n + 1L
      }
    }

    A <- as.integer(runif(N) < pi_engage)
    reward_success <- as.integer(runif(N) < p_reward)
    reward_observed <- A * reward_success * reward_mag

    V <- V + alpha_V * A * (reward_observed - V)
    C <- C - alpha_C * A * (C - C_min)

    V <- clip(V, lo = 0, hi = reward_mag)
    C <- pmax(C, C_min)
  }

  early_scores <- early_child_sum / early_child_n
  middle_scores <- middle_child_sum / middle_child_n
  late_scores <- late_child_sum / late_child_n

  early_mean <- early_sum / early_n
  late_mean <- late_sum / late_n
  early_sd <- early_sd_sum / early_sd_n
  late_sd <- late_sd_sum / late_sd_n

  tibble(
    early_mean = early_mean,
    late_mean = late_mean,
    delta_mean = late_mean - early_mean,
    early_sd = early_sd,
    late_sd = late_sd,
    sd_gain = late_sd - early_sd,
    rho_middle_late = suppressWarnings(
      cor(middle_scores, late_scores, method = "spearman")
    ),
    rho_early_late = suppressWarnings(
      cor(early_scores, late_scores, method = "spearman")
    )
  )
}

rank_percentile <- function(x) {
  if (length(unique(x)) <= 1) return(rep(0.5, length(x)))
  dplyr::percent_rank(x)
}

# Fail loudly if a time-series plot is accidentally truncated or contains
# non-finite values. This is used before the main developmental figures.
assert_plot_coverage <- function(
  df,
  time_col = "step",
  group_cols = character(0),
  value_cols = NULL,
  expected_start = 1,
  expected_end = default_pars$T,
  tolerance = 1e-6
) {

  stopifnot(time_col %in% names(df))

  if (length(group_cols) == 0) {
    ranges <- tibble(
      min_time = min(df[[time_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      max_time = max(df[[time_col]], na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  } else {
    ranges <- df %>%
      group_by(across(all_of(group_cols))) %>%
      summarize(
        min_time = min(.data[[time_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
        max_time = max(.data[[time_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
      )
  }

  if (
    any(abs(ranges$min_time - expected_start) > tolerance) ||
    any(abs(ranges$max_time - expected_end) > tolerance)
  ) {
    stop("A plotted trajectory does not span the intended time range.")
  }

  if (!is.null(value_cols)) {
    bad <- vapply(
      value_cols,
      function(v) any(!is.finite(df[[v]])),
      logical(1)
    )
    if (any(bad)) {
      stop(
        "Non-finite values found in plotted variables: ",
        paste(value_cols[bad], collapse = ", ")
      )
    }
  }

  invisible(TRUE)
}

score_at_steps <- function(df, center_step, half_width) {
  df %>%
    filter(
      step >= center_step - half_width,
      step <= center_step + half_width
    ) %>%
    group_by(child_id) %>%
    summarize(score = mean(pi), .groups = "drop")
}
```

# Result 1: Practice feedback changes the developmental dynamics

We first compare nested models using agents who are **identical at baseline and share the same reward environment**. The point is to identify which mechanism is actually responsible for developmental change and differentiation.

```{r}
#| label: run_nested_models
#| echo: true

core_models <- c(
  "evc",
  "value",
  "value_cost"
)

df_models <- bind_rows(
  lapply(seq_along(core_models), function(j) {
    simulate_population(
      model = core_models[j],
      p_reward_sd = 0,
      seed = 4100
    )
  })
)

summary_models <- population_summary(df_models)

assert_plot_coverage(
  summary_models,
  group_cols = "model_label",
  value_cols = c("mean_pi", "sd_pi")
)

model_metrics <- bind_rows(
  lapply(split(df_models, df_models$model_label), function(x) {
    development_metrics(x)
  }),
  .id = "model_label"
)
```

## Population mean and between-child heterogeneity

```{r}
#| label: fig_nested_models
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| fig-align: center

nested_plot_df <- summary_models %>%
  select(model_label, step, mean_pi, sd_pi) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_pi, sd_pi),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      mean_pi = "Population mean propensity",
      sd_pi = "Between-child SD in propensity"
    )
  )

ggplot(
  nested_plot_df,
  aes(step, value, color = model_label)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_cols) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "What does each mechanism add?",
    subtitle = "All agents start identically and share the same reward environment",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = NULL,
    color = NULL
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: table_nested_metrics
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  model_metrics %>%
    select(model_label, early_mean, late_mean, early_sd, late_sd, rho_middle_late),
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Model",
    "Early mean",
    "Late mean",
    "Early SD",
    "Late SD",
    "Middle-to-late rank persistence (Spearman rho)"
  ),
  caption = "Developmental change, heterogeneity, and rank persistence by model"
)
```

The last column asks whether children who are relatively high or low in engagement during the **middle** of the simulated period tend to remain relatively high or low **later**. It is the Spearman rank correlation between each child's middle-stage and late-stage mean engagement propensity. With the default $T=1500$, the middle window is approximately $t=750$--$900$ and the late window is approximately $t=1275$--$1425$. A larger positive $\rho$ means stronger persistence of the children's relative ordering. M0 is `NA` because all children remain identical, so there is no between-child ranking to correlate.

With the current provisional parameters, **EVC alone is flat**, as expected: there is no learning mechanism that could generate developmental change. Adding learned value produces some change, but the much larger shift appears after adding the practice feedback. In M2, children who happen to engage slightly more receive more opportunities both to update value and to reduce future subjective cost.

The reinforcing part of the mechanism is

$$
\pi_t\uparrow
\rightarrow
A_t\uparrow
\rightarrow
\begin{cases}
\text{more reward-learning opportunities}\\
\text{more practice-related cost reduction}
\end{cases}
\rightarrow
\pi_{t+1}\uparrow.
$$

This does **not** imply unlimited divergence. As $V_t$ approaches the average payoff available in the environment and $C_t$ approaches $C_{\min}$, there is progressively less left to learn or improve, so the feedback weakens.

# Result 2: Initially identical children differentiate over development

This is the strictest emergence test. Everyone has

$$
V_{i,0}=V_0,
\qquad
C_{i,0}=C_0,
\qquad
p_i=p.
$$

The only source of between-child differences is chance variation in (1) whether EF is actually engaged and (2) whether engagement pays off. No between-child variation in engagement propensity is specified at baseline: because all children begin with the same $V_0$, $C_0$, and parameters, they also begin with the same $\pi_{i,0}$ and therefore $SD(\pi_{i,0})=0$. Any later between-child SD in engagement propensity is an **emergent outcome** of their different realized engagement and reward histories, not an input parameter.

```{r}
#| label: run_identical_population
#| echo: true

df_identical <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 1000,
  p_reward_sd = 0,
  seed = 20260819
)

metrics_identical <- development_metrics(df_identical)
stability_identical <- stability_table(df_identical)
```

## Example individual trajectories

A population summary can hide the fact that the model is producing genuinely different developmental paths. The next figure shows 15 example children from the **identical-start, identical-environment** simulation. The labels "lower," "middle," and "higher late engagement" are assigned **after the simulation** according to each child's average engagement propensity during the late window: children in the lower, middle, and upper thirds are labeled accordingly. These groups are used only to select and color illustrative trajectories; they are not model inputs, and no high-, middle-, or low-engagement groups are specified in advance.

```{r}
#| label: fig_identical_trajectories
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-align: center
#| message: false

late_groups_identical <- df_identical %>%
  filter(step >= episode_at_fraction(max(step), 0.85), step <= episode_at_fraction(max(step), 0.95)) %>%
  group_by(child_id) %>%
  summarize(
    late_pi = mean(pi),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    late_group = case_when(
      late_pi <= quantile(late_pi, 1/3) ~ "Lower late engagement",
      late_pi >= quantile(late_pi, 2/3) ~ "Higher late engagement",
      TRUE ~ "Middle late engagement"
    )
  )

set.seed(20260820)

sample_n_safe <- function(df, k = 5) {
  dplyr::slice_sample(
    df,
    n = min(k, nrow(df))
  )
}

sampled_children <- bind_rows(
  late_groups_identical %>%
    filter(late_group == "Lower late engagement") %>%
    sample_n_safe(5),
  late_groups_identical %>%
    filter(late_group == "Middle late engagement") %>%
    sample_n_safe(5),
  late_groups_identical %>%
    filter(late_group == "Higher late engagement") %>%
    sample_n_safe(5)
)

trajectory_df <- df_identical %>%
  semi_join(sampled_children, by = "child_id") %>%
  left_join(
    sampled_children %>%
      select(child_id, late_group),
    by = "child_id"
  )

trajectory_mean <- df_identical %>%
  group_by(step) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_pi = mean(pi),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

trajectory_cols <- c(
  "Lower late engagement" = "#4E79A7",
  "Middle late engagement" = "#7A7A7A",
  "Higher late engagement" = "#D62728"
)

ggplot(
  trajectory_df,
  aes(step, pi, group = child_id, color = late_group)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.55, linewidth = 0.70) +
  geom_line(
    data = trajectory_mean,
    aes(step, mean_pi),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 1.15
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = trajectory_cols) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Different developmental paths emerge from identical starts",
    subtitle = "Same starting states and environment; differences arise only from chance differences in experience",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = "EF engagement propensity",
    color = NULL
  )
```

Even when every child begins with the same parameters, the same initial engagement propensity, and the same reward environment, chance differences in engagement decisions and reward outcomes generate visibly different developmental paths.

For visualization only, children are grouped **after the simulation** according to their average late-stage engagement propensity: lower third, middle third, or upper third. Five trajectories from each group are shown. These labels are therefore descriptive rather than model inputs; no high-, middle-, or low-engagement groups are specified in advance. Because the groups are defined by late engagement, their separation near the end of the figure is partly true by construction. The figure is intended to illustrate how different developmental paths can emerge from identical starting conditions, not to establish rank persistence. Persistence is evaluated separately below using rank correlations.

These differences are substantial over the developmental horizon, although the shared-environment long-horizon analysis below shows that their identities are not permanently fixed.

## The population spreads out

```{r}
#| label: fig_emerging_distribution
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5.0
#| fig-align: center

snapshots <- bind_rows(
  get_snapshot(df_identical, 0.25, "Early"),
  get_snapshot(df_identical, 0.55, "Middle"),
  get_snapshot(df_identical, 0.90, "Late")
) %>%
  mutate(
    snapshot = factor(
      snapshot,
      levels = c("Early", "Middle", "Late")
    )
  )

ggplot(snapshots, aes(pi, color = snapshot)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1.05, adjust = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = snapshot_cols) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "An initially homogeneous population spreads out",
    subtitle = "No between-child parameter or environmental differences are imposed",
    x = "EF engagement propensity",
    y = "Density",
    color = NULL
  )
```

The increase in dispersion is substantial over this developmental horizon. The between-child spread in engagement propensity is generated by the model rather than imposed at baseline.

<details>
<summary><strong>How is the between-child SD in engagement propensity generated?</strong></summary>

All children begin with the same $V_0$, $C_0$, parameters, and reward environment. They therefore also begin with the same engagement propensity,

$$
\pi_{i,0}
=
\sigma\!\left(\frac{V_0-C_0}{\tau}\right),
$$

so initially

$$
SD_i(\pi_{i,0})=0.
$$

The randomness enters through the actual engagement decision and reward outcome:

$$
A_{i,t}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{i,t}),
\qquad
Y_{i,t}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p).
$$

Thus, two children with exactly the same propensity can nevertheless have different experiences on a given episode: one may engage while the other does not, and among children who engage, one may be rewarded while another is not. Those different experiences update $V_{i,t}$ and $C_{i,t}$ differently, which then produces different propensities on later episodes.

The reported between-child SD at episode $t$ is simply calculated from the propensities generated for the population:

$$
SD_i(\pi_{i,t})
=
\sqrt{
\frac{1}{N-1}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left(\pi_{i,t}-\bar{\pi}_t\right)^2
}.
$$

It is therefore an **output of the model, not a free parameter**. Its magnitude depends on the learning and practice parameters ($\alpha_V$, $\alpha_C$), decision sensitivity ($\tau$), the reward environment ($p$ and reward magnitude), the starting states and practice floor, and how long chance differences in experience have had to accumulate.

This between-child SD is different from the Bernoulli variance $\pi_{i,t}(1-\pi_{i,t})$. The latter describes uncertainty in whether one child engages on a particular episode; the former describes how far apart children's underlying engagement propensities have become.

</details>

This establishes **heterogeneity**, but not yet permanent individual types.

## Relative differences are moderately persistent

```{r}
#| label: table_rank_stability
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  stability_identical,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Rank-order stability of EF engagement propensity"
)
```

The rank correlations are moderate rather than close to 1. We therefore describe these differences as **developmentally persistent** or **moderately rank-stable**, not as permanently fixed individual differences.

### Rank-to-rank visualization

The previous propensity-versus-propensity scatter was dominated by the fact that the whole population improves. A percentile plot isolates the question we actually care about: whether children preserve their relative position.

A **rank percentile** describes where a child stands relative to the other children at the same developmental period, rather than their absolute engagement propensity. A value near 0 means the child is among the lowest in the population, 0.50 means roughly the middle, and a value near 1 means among the highest. For example, a rank percentile of 0.75 means that the child's engagement propensity is higher than that of about 75% of the other children.

```{r}
#| label: fig_rank_stability
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-align: center

scores_identical <- bind_rows(
  window_score(df_identical, 0.50, 0.60, "Middle"),
  window_score(df_identical, 0.85, 0.95, "Late")
) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = window,
    values_from = score
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    middle_rank = rank_percentile(Middle),
    late_rank = rank_percentile(Late)
  )

ggplot(scores_identical, aes(middle_rank, late_rank)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.28, size = 1.3) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "How much rank ordering persists?",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Middle-to-late Spearman rho = ",
      round(stability_identical$spearman_rho[
        stability_identical$comparison == "Middle vs Late"
      ], 2)
    ),
    x = "Middle-stage rank percentile",
    y = "Late-stage rank percentile"
  )
```

Each point represents one child. The x-axis gives that child's relative rank during the middle stage, and the y-axis gives the same child's relative rank during the late stage. The dashed diagonal represents perfect rank preservation: a child on this line occupies the same relative position at both periods. Points above the line moved upward relative to other children, whereas points below the line moved downward.

The middle-to-late Spearman correlation summarizes this pattern. A value of about $\rho=0.62$ indicates **moderate rank persistence**: children who are relatively high in the middle tend to remain relatively high later, and children who are relatively low tend to remain relatively low, but there is substantial reshuffling. Because the axes use ranks rather than raw propensity, this comparison is not driven by the overall increase in engagement across the population.


### Do these differences last indefinitely?

Result 2 shows that initially identical children can become meaningfully different over the main developmental simulation. A separate question is whether those differences remain tied to the same children forever when everyone continues to experience the **same** reward environment.

To check this, we continue simulating the same initially identical children for four times longer than in the main simulation.

```{r}
#| label: run_long_horizon
#| echo: true

T_long <- 4 * (default_pars$T - 1) + 1

df_long <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 600,
  T = T_long,
  p_reward_sd = 0,
  record_every = 10,
  seed = 1400
)
```

There are two useful questions.

**1. How far apart are children at a given time?**

```{r}
#| label: fig_long_sd
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

long_sd <- df_long %>%
  group_by(step) %>%
  summarize(sd_pi = sd(pi), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(long_sd, aes(step, sd_pi)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = default_pars$T,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Between-child differences grow, then gradually decrease",
    subtitle = "Dashed line marks the end of the main developmental simulation",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = "Between-child SD in engagement propensity"
  )
```

The population first spreads out, as shown in Result 2. Over a much longer period, that spread begins to decrease. Some variation remains because engagement and reward outcomes continue to be probabilistic.

**2. Do the same children remain relatively high or low?**

We take each child's average engagement near the end of the main developmental simulation and ask how strongly that ranking predicts the child's ranking later.

```{r}
#| label: rank_memory_long
#| echo: true

reference_rank_scores <- df_long %>%
  filter(
    step >= round(0.80 * (default_pars$T - 1)) + 1,
    step <= round(0.95 * (default_pars$T - 1)) + 1
  ) %>%
  group_by(child_id) %>%
  summarize(reference_score = mean(pi), .groups = "drop")

memory_centers <- seq(0.90, 4.00, by = 0.20)
memory_half_width <- 0.06

rank_memory <- bind_rows(
  lapply(memory_centers, function(center_i) {

    center_step <- round(center_i * (default_pars$T - 1)) + 1
    half_width_steps <- round(memory_half_width * (default_pars$T - 1))

    later_scores <- df_long %>%
      filter(
        step >= center_step - half_width_steps,
        step <= center_step + half_width_steps
      ) %>%
      group_by(child_id) %>%
      summarize(later_score = mean(pi), .groups = "drop")

    joined <- inner_join(
      reference_rank_scores,
      later_scores,
      by = "child_id"
    )

    tibble(
      episode = center_step,
      rank_memory = cor(
        joined$reference_score,
        joined$later_score,
        method = "spearman"
      )
    )
  })
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig_rank_memory_long
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(rank_memory, aes(episode, rank_memory)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.1, 1)) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Earlier high/low rankings gradually lose predictive value",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = "Spearman rank correlation with earlier ranking"
  )
```

So under a completely shared environment, chance differences in experience can create substantial and fairly persistent developmental differences, but they do **not** permanently divide children into fixed high- and low-engagement groups. This is why Result 3 asks what changes when children experience small but persistent differences in how often EF pays off.


# Result 3: Persistent reward differences make later engagement differences more stable

Result 2 deliberately gave every child the same reward environment. In development, however, children may differ slightly and consistently in how often engaging EF pays off.

We represent this by allowing the stable reward probability $p_i$ to vary across children while keeping all other between-child parameters identical.

The amount of variation is not empirically estimated here. Rather than choosing one value and treating it as special, we test:

$$
SD(p_i)\in\{0,\ .01,\ .02,\ .04,\ .06\}.
$$

Here $SD(p_i)=0$ is the shared-environment case from Result 2. Larger values mean that children differ more in how often EF engagement tends to be rewarded.

## Does more persistent environmental variation make rank differences more stable?

For each value of $SD(p_i)$, we measure:

1. **late between-child spread:** the SD of children's engagement propensities late in the simulation;
2. **middle-to-late rank persistence:** whether children who are relatively high or low in the middle tend to remain relatively high or low later.

The rank-persistence measure is the main outcome here. The late between-child SD is retained in the table as a descriptive check.

```{r}
#| label: reward_sd_sensitivity
#| echo: true
#| message: false

reward_sd_grid <- c(0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06)

reward_sd_sensitivity <- map_dfr(
  reward_sd_grid,
  function(sd_p) {

    df_sd <- simulate_population(
      model = "value_cost",
      N = 1000,
      p_reward_sd = sd_p,
      seed = 601
    )

    metrics_sd <- development_metrics(df_sd)

    tibble(
      imposed_sd_p = sd_p,
      late_sd_pi = metrics_sd$late_sd,
      rho_middle_late = metrics_sd$rho_middle_late
    )
  }
)

reward_sd_sensitivity_display <- reward_sd_sensitivity %>%
  transmute(
    `Imposed SD(p_i)` = imposed_sd_p,
    `Late SD in engagement propensity` = late_sd_pi,
    `Middle-to-late rank persistence (Spearman rho)` = rho_middle_late
  )

knitr::kable(
  reward_sd_sensitivity_display,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Effect of persistent between-child differences in reward probability"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig_reward_sd_sensitivity_rank
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(
  reward_sd_sensitivity,
  aes(imposed_sd_p, rho_middle_late)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.60, 0.90)) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Persistent reward differences make rank ordering more stable",
    subtitle = "Middle-to-late Spearman rank correlation",
    x = "Between-child SD in reward probability",
    y = "Middle-to-late rank persistence"
  )
```

As persistent differences in reward probability get larger, children's relative engagement rankings become more stable over time. The overall between-child spread also increases, but that is the more obvious consequence of imposing greater variation in $p_i$ and is therefore not the main result.

The main point of this sensitivity analysis is that the increase in rank persistence is **gradual rather than specific to the illustrative choice $SD(p_i)=0.02$**.

## Why can persistent reward differences matter in the long run?

With a shared reward probability $p$, all children have the same long-run mean payoff target. With child-specific reward probabilities,

$$
V_i^*=p_i r,
$$

so children with different $p_i$ need not have the same long-run mean engagement propensity:

$$
\pi_i^*
=
\sigma\!\left(
\frac{p_i r-C_{\min}}{\tau}
\right).
$$

The next figure uses $SD(p_i)=0.02$ only as a **small illustrative condition**. It is one point on the sensitivity analysis above, not an empirically calibrated value.

```{r}
#| label: fig_environment_long_trajectories
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-align: center
#| message: false

T_long_env <- 4 * (default_pars$T - 1) + 1

df_environment_long <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 1000,
  T = T_long_env,
  p_reward_sd = 0.02,
  record_every = 10,
  seed = 601
)

environment_groups <- df_environment_long %>%
  distinct(
    child_id,
    p_reward_child
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    environment_group = case_when(
      p_reward_child <= quantile(p_reward_child, 1/3) ~
        "Less rewarding environment",
      p_reward_child >= quantile(p_reward_child, 2/3) ~
        "More rewarding environment",
      TRUE ~
        "Intermediate environment"
    )
  )

set.seed(20260820)

sampled_environment_children <- bind_rows(
  environment_groups %>%
    filter(environment_group == "Less rewarding environment") %>%
    sample_n_safe(5),
  environment_groups %>%
    filter(environment_group == "Intermediate environment") %>%
    sample_n_safe(5),
  environment_groups %>%
    filter(environment_group == "More rewarding environment") %>%
    sample_n_safe(5)
)

trajectory_environment <- df_environment_long %>%
  semi_join(
    sampled_environment_children,
    by = "child_id"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    sampled_environment_children %>%
      select(child_id, environment_group),
    by = "child_id"
  )

environment_group_mean <- df_environment_long %>%
  left_join(
    environment_groups,
    by = c("child_id", "p_reward_child")
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    environment_group,
    step
  ) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_pi = mean(pi),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

environment_cols <- c(
  "Less rewarding environment" = "#4E79A7",
  "Intermediate environment" = "#7A7A7A",
  "More rewarding environment" = "#D62728"
)

ggplot(
  trajectory_environment,
  aes(
    step,
    pi,
    group = child_id,
    color = environment_group
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    alpha = 0.26,
    linewidth = 0.48
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = environment_group_mean,
    aes(
      step,
      mean_pi,
      color = environment_group,
      group = environment_group
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.45
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = default_pars$T,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.55
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = environment_cols) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Small persistent reward differences lead to different long-run mean engagement levels",
    subtitle = "Groups are defined by children's stable reward probabilities; all other parameters are shared",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = "EF engagement propensity",
    color = NULL
  )
```

The thin lines are example children; the thicker lines are group averages. The groups are defined by the lower, middle, and upper thirds of the child-specific reward probabilities $p_i$. The point is not that $SD(p_i)=0.02$ creates dramatically more spread. Rather, a persistent difference in the reward environment gives children systematically different long-run mean payoff values, which can help maintain differences in engagement.

# Result 4: Temporary stress produces a temporary drop in EF engagement

Stress enters the **fast decision** through the temporary contextual cost $X_t$:

$$
D_t
=
V_t-C_t-X_t.
$$

During a stressor,

$$
X_t\uparrow
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\pi_t\downarrow.
$$

Stress does not directly change the learned payoff $V_t$ or learned effort cost $C_t$. Any small difference that remains afterward arises indirectly because reduced engagement means fewer reward-learning and practice opportunities during the stress period.

```{r}
#| label: run_stress
#| echo: true

T_stress <- default_pars$T

stress_vec <- rep(0, T_stress)
stress_start <- round(0.55 * T_stress)
stress_end <- round(0.585 * T_stress)
stress_vec[stress_start:stress_end] <- 0.20

df_no_stress <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 1000,
  extra_cost = rep(0, T_stress),
  seed = 810
) %>%
  mutate(condition = "Reference")

df_stress <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 1000,
  extra_cost = stress_vec,
  seed = 810
) %>%
  mutate(condition = "Temporary stress")

df_stress_all <- bind_rows(
  df_no_stress,
  df_stress
)

stress_summary <- df_stress_all %>%
  group_by(condition, step) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_X = mean(extra_cost),
    mean_pi = mean(pi),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## Immediate effect

```{r}
#| label: fig_stress_main
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 5.8
#| fig-align: center

stress_main <- stress_summary %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_X, mean_pi),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      mean_X = "1. Temporary contextual cost X(t)",
      mean_pi = "2. EF engagement propensity"
    )
  )

ggplot(
  stress_main,
  aes(step, value, color = condition)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(stress_start, stress_end),
    linetype = "dotted",
    linewidth = 0.45,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Reference" = "#4B5563",
      "Temporary stress" = "#B54A4A"
    )
  ) +
  theme_result(base_size = 13) +
  labs(
    title = "Temporary stress causes a sharp but temporary engagement dip",
    subtitle = "Dotted lines mark the stress period",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = NULL,
    color = NULL
  )
```

The main effect is immediate: engagement propensity drops sharply while the stressor is present and then rebounds once the stressor ends.

## Is there any difference left after the stressor ends?

The remaining difference is much smaller than the acute drop, so we show only the **post-stress period** on a tighter y-axis.

```{r}
#| label: fig_stress_residual
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

stress_post <- stress_summary %>%
  filter(
    condition %in% c("Reference", "Temporary stress"),
    step > stress_end
  ) %>%
  select(condition, step, mean_pi)

stress_residual_wide <- stress_post %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = condition,
    values_from = mean_pi
  )

late_window_start_stress <- round(0.85 * T_stress)

late_residual <- stress_residual_wide %>%
  filter(step >= late_window_start_stress) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_delta = mean(`Temporary stress` - Reference)
  ) %>%
  pull(mean_delta)

ggplot(
  stress_post,
  aes(step, mean_pi, color = condition)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.0) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Reference" = "#4B5563",
      "Temporary stress" = "#B54A4A"
    )
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = range(stress_post$mean_pi, na.rm = TRUE) + c(-0.002, 0.002)
  ) +
  theme_result(base_size = 13) +
  labs(
    title = "Only a small separation remains after stress ends",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Late-window mean difference (stress - reference) = ",
      round(late_residual, 3)
    ),
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = "Mean EF engagement propensity",
    color = NULL
  )
```

This zoomed view keeps the original two trajectories rather than plotting their difference directly. It shows that after the stressor ends, the stress condition remains slightly below the reference trajectory. In this model, that residual gap comes from reduced learning and practice during the stress period. The main result remains the **temporary engagement dip**, not a large lasting effect.

# Result 5: The minimal model does not give early support a special advantage

The model allows experience to change later engagement, but that does not automatically mean that **earlier** experience has a stronger effect than the same experience later.

We test this by increasing the reward probability by the same amount for the same duration, once early and once later in the simulation.

```{r}
#| label: run_reward_timing
#| echo: true

T_reward <- default_pars$T

reward_early <- rep(0, T_reward)
reward_late <- rep(0, T_reward)

duration <- round(0.13 * T_reward)
boost <- 0.12

early_start <- round(0.20 * T_reward)
late_start <- round(0.60 * T_reward)

early_end <- early_start + duration - 1
late_end <- late_start + duration - 1

reward_early[early_start:early_end] <- boost
reward_late[late_start:late_end] <- boost

df_reward_ref <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 1000,
  p_reward_shift = rep(0, T_reward),
  seed = 910
) %>%
  mutate(condition = "Reference")

df_reward_early <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 1000,
  p_reward_shift = reward_early,
  seed = 910
) %>%
  mutate(condition = "Early support")

df_reward_late <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 1000,
  p_reward_shift = reward_late,
  seed = 910
) %>%
  mutate(condition = "Later support")

df_reward_timing <- bind_rows(
  df_reward_ref,
  df_reward_early,
  df_reward_late
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig_reward_timing
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 5.8
#| fig-align: center

reward_summary <- df_reward_timing %>%
  group_by(condition, step) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_p = mean(p_reward_used),
    mean_pi = mean(pi),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_p, mean_pi),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      mean_p = "1. Reward probability",
      mean_pi = "2. EF engagement propensity"
    )
  )

ggplot(
  reward_summary,
  aes(step, value, color = condition)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.0) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Reference" = "#4B5563",
      "Early support" = "#B54A4A",
      "Later support" = "#3B82B6"
    )
  ) +
  theme_result(base_size = 13) +
  labs(
    title = "The same reward support is given early or later",
    subtitle = "The lower panel shows the resulting change in EF engagement propensity",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = NULL,
    color = NULL
  )
```

## How should early and later support be compared?

If we measure both interventions at the **final episode**, later support has occurred more recently, so that comparison can favor the later intervention simply because less time has passed.

The more informative comparison is therefore to measure each intervention after the **same amount of follow-up time** has elapsed since it ended.

```{r}
#| label: reward_timing_comparisons
#| echo: true

# Common final developmental window
final_start <- round(0.85 * T_reward)

final_effects <- df_reward_timing %>%
  filter(step >= final_start) %>%
  group_by(condition) %>%
  summarize(mean_pi = mean(pi), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = mean_pi) %>%
  transmute(
    comparison = "Common final time",
    early_effect = `Early support` - Reference,
    later_effect = `Later support` - Reference
  )

# Equal follow-up lag after each intervention ends
followup_lag <- round(0.15 * T_reward)
window_halfwidth <- round(0.025 * T_reward)

early_eval_center <- early_end + followup_lag
late_eval_center <- late_end + followup_lag

window_mean <- function(df, condition_name, center, halfwidth) {
  df %>%
    filter(
      condition == condition_name,
      step >= center - halfwidth,
      step <= center + halfwidth
    ) %>%
    summarize(value = mean(pi)) %>%
    pull(value)
}

early_effect_equal_lag <-
  window_mean(df_reward_timing, "Early support", early_eval_center, window_halfwidth) -
  window_mean(df_reward_timing, "Reference", early_eval_center, window_halfwidth)

later_effect_equal_lag <-
  window_mean(df_reward_timing, "Later support", late_eval_center, window_halfwidth) -
  window_mean(df_reward_timing, "Reference", late_eval_center, window_halfwidth)

equal_lag_effects <- tibble(
  comparison = "Same follow-up lag",
  early_effect = early_effect_equal_lag,
  later_effect = later_effect_equal_lag
)

reward_timing_effects <- bind_rows(
  final_effects,
  equal_lag_effects
)

knitr::kable(
  reward_timing_effects,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Comparison",
    "Effect of early support",
    "Effect of later support"
  ),
  caption = "Early versus later support"
)
```

The **same-follow-up-lag** comparison is the key one. Under the current default parameters, early and later support have very similar effects once the amount of follow-up time is matched. The model therefore does not produce an inherent early-support advantage.

This is theoretically useful: experience-dependent feedback can make experience matter without automatically creating a sensitive period. If we want early experience to be systematically more influential than the same later experience, the model would need an additional developmental mechanism, such as age-dependent plasticity.

# Result 6: Do the main results depend on the parameter choices?

The previous results use one provisional set of parameter values. We therefore ask whether the same qualitative pattern appears when those assumptions are changed.

We generate **250 different parameter combinations**. For each combination, we simulate **five independent populations** so that one unusual random run is not mistaken for a parameter effect.

The table below shows exactly what is varied. The ranges are theoretical sensitivity ranges rather than empirically estimated bounds.

| Parameter | Meaning | Default value | Values sampled in the sensitivity analysis | Sampling |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| $\alpha_V$ | How quickly expected payoff is learned | 0.0244 | 0.006 to 0.070 | log-uniform |
| $\alpha_C$ | How quickly practice reduces future effort cost | 0.00263 | 0.0004 to 0.0070 | log-uniform |
| $\tau$ | How strongly net value differences translate into engagement probability | 0.163 | 0.10 to 0.30 | uniform |
| $p$ | Probability that EF engagement pays off for everyone in that simulated population | 0.591 | 0.45 to 0.72 | uniform |
| $D_0=V_0-C_0$ | Initial net value of engaging EF | -0.410 | -0.60 to -0.20 | uniform |
| $C_0-C_{\min}$ | Maximum amount of practice-related cost reduction available | 0.528 | 0.25 to 0.75 | uniform |

For each of the 250 parameter sets, the six values are sampled independently from these ranges. The two learning rates are sampled on a **log scale** because their plausible sensitivity ranges span roughly an order of magnitude; the remaining parameters are sampled uniformly over the stated intervals.

Each parameter set is then simulated five times with independent random engagement and reward histories. In the full sweep, each simulated population contains **150 children followed for 900 developmental episodes**. The five replications are averaged before comparing parameter sets.

Within any one parameter set, children still begin identically and share the same reward probability $p$. Thus, this analysis varies the **general model assumptions across simulated populations**. It is different from Result 3, where the mean reward environment is held fixed but $p_i$ varies **between children within the same population**.

```{r}
#| label: run_parameter_sweep
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

log_runif <- function(n, min, max) {
  exp(runif(n, log(min), log(max)))
}

set.seed(260819)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sweep size
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Use quick_sweep = TRUE while developing the document.
# Set it to FALSE for the full analysis used in the final results.
quick_sweep <- FALSE

if (quick_sweep) {
  n_parameter_sets <- 80
  n_mc_reps <- 3
  sweep_N <- 100
  sweep_T <- 700
} else {
  n_parameter_sets <- 250
  n_mc_reps <- 5
  sweep_N <- 150
  sweep_T <- 900
}

sweep_pars <- tibble(
  set_id = seq_len(n_parameter_sets),

  alpha_V = log_runif(n_parameter_sets, 0.006, 0.070),
  alpha_C = log_runif(n_parameter_sets, 0.0004, 0.0070),
  tau = runif(n_parameter_sets, 0.10, 0.30),
  p_reward = runif(n_parameter_sets, 0.45, 0.72),

  # Initial net value and future practice opportunity are varied separately.
  initial_delta = runif(n_parameter_sets, -0.60, -0.20),
  practice_range = runif(n_parameter_sets, 0.25, 0.75),

  V0 = default_pars$V0
) %>%
  mutate(
    C0 = V0 - initial_delta,
    C_min = C0 - practice_range
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Parallel execution
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Parallelize over parameter sets. Each worker runs the Monte Carlo
# replications for one parameter vector sequentially. This avoids the
# overhead of launching one future for every single replication.
#
# On macOS/Linux the sweep uses base R forked workers.
# Leave one physical core free for the operating system.
n_workers <- max(
  1L,
  min(
    n_parameter_sets,
    parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE) - 1L
  )
)

# Fallback for machines where physical-core detection returns NA/1.
if (is.na(n_workers) || n_workers < 1L) n_workers <- 1L

message(
  "Parameter sweep: ",
  n_parameter_sets, " parameter sets × ",
  n_mc_reps, " replications; ",
  n_workers, " parallel workers."
)

sweep_list <- parallel_lapply(
  seq_len(n_parameter_sets),

  function(j) {

    pars_j <- sweep_pars[j, ]

    bind_rows(
      lapply(seq_len(n_mc_reps), function(mc) {

        metrics_j <- simulate_development_metrics_fast(
          N = sweep_N,
          T = sweep_T,

          V0 = pars_j$V0,
          C0 = pars_j$C0,
          C_min = pars_j$C_min,

          tau = pars_j$tau,
          p_reward = pars_j$p_reward,
          alpha_V = pars_j$alpha_V,
          alpha_C = pars_j$alpha_C,

          record_every = 10,
          seed = 100000 + j * 100 + mc
        )

        bind_cols(
          pars_j,
          tibble(mc_rep = mc),
          metrics_j
        )
      })
    )
  },

  workers = n_workers
)

sweep_rep_results <- bind_rows(sweep_list)

# Average each outcome across independent simulation realizations.
sweep_results <- sweep_rep_results %>%
  group_by(
    set_id,
    alpha_V,
    alpha_C,
    tau,
    p_reward,
    initial_delta,
    practice_range,
    V0,
    C0,
    C_min
  ) %>%
  summarize(
    # Keep replication-level names intact while computing uncertainty.
    delta_mean_avg = mean(delta_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    delta_mean_mc_sd = sd(delta_mean, na.rm = TRUE),

    sd_gain_avg = mean(sd_gain, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_gain_mc_sd = sd(sd_gain, na.rm = TRUE),

    rho_middle_late_avg = mean(rho_middle_late, na.rm = TRUE),
    rho_middle_late_mc_sd = sd(rho_middle_late, na.rm = TRUE),

    rho_early_late_avg = mean(rho_early_late, na.rm = TRUE),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  rename(
    delta_mean = delta_mean_avg,
    sd_gain = sd_gain_avg,
    rho_middle_late = rho_middle_late_avg,
    rho_early_late = rho_early_late_avg
  )
```

For each parameter combination, we ask three simple questions:

1. Does average engagement increase from early to late development?
2. Does between-child variation increase from early to late development?
3. Once children have begun to differ, how strongly does their middle-stage ranking predict their later ranking?

The first two questions can be shown together in one figure. Each point below is **one parameter combination**, averaged across its five independent simulated populations.

```{r}
#| label: fig_parameter_robustness
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 6.4
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

sweep_patterns <- sweep_results %>%
  mutate(
    pattern = case_when(
      delta_mean > 0 & sd_gain > 0 ~ "Improvement + differentiation",
      delta_mean > 0 & sd_gain <= 0 ~ "Improvement only",
      delta_mean <= 0 & sd_gain > 0 ~ "Differentiation only",
      TRUE ~ "Neither"
    )
  )

pattern_levels <- c(
  "Improvement + differentiation",
  "Improvement only",
  "Differentiation only",
  "Neither"
)

pattern_counts <- sweep_patterns %>%
  count(pattern) %>%
  tidyr::complete(
    pattern = pattern_levels,
    fill = list(n = 0)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    pct = n / sum(n)
  )

x_right <- max(sweep_patterns$delta_mean, na.rm = TRUE)
x_left  <- min(sweep_patterns$delta_mean, na.rm = TRUE)
y_top   <- max(sweep_patterns$sd_gain, na.rm = TRUE)
y_bottom <- min(sweep_patterns$sd_gain, na.rm = TRUE)

label_positions <- tibble(
  pattern = pattern_levels,
  x = c(
    0.70 * x_right,
    0.70 * x_right,
    0.70 * x_left,
    0.70 * x_left
  ),
  y = c(
    0.82 * y_top,
    0.72 * y_bottom,
    0.82 * y_top,
    0.72 * y_bottom
  )
) %>%
  left_join(pattern_counts, by = "pattern") %>%
  mutate(
    label = paste0(
      pattern,
      "\n",
      scales::percent(pct, accuracy = 1)
    )
  )

ggplot(
  sweep_patterns,
  aes(delta_mean, sd_gain)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.42,
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = label_positions,
    aes(x, y, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.6,
    lineheight = 0.95
  ) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Do developmental improvement and differentiation survive parameter changes?",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Each point is one parameter combination, averaged across ",
      n_mc_reps,
      " independent simulated populations"
    ),
    x = "Change in mean EF engagement (late - early)",
    y = "Change in between-child SD (late - early)"
  )
```

How to read the figure:

- **upper right:** average engagement increases and children become more different;
- **lower right:** average engagement increases, but between-child variation does not;
- **upper left:** children become more different, but average engagement does not increase;
- **lower left:** neither pattern occurs.

The upper-right quadrant is therefore the parameter region that reproduces the two main developmental findings from Results 1 and 2.

Rank persistence is not encoded in this figure because adding a third visual dimension makes the plot harder to read. We summarize it separately in the table below.

```{r}
#| label: table_parameter_robustness
#| echo: false

robustness_summary <- tibble(
  `Question` = c(
    "Does mean EF engagement increase?",
    "Does between-child variation increase?",
    "Do both occur together?",
    "How persistent is middle-to-late rank ordering?"
  ),
  `Summary across parameter sets` = c(
    scales::percent(
      mean(sweep_results$delta_mean > 0),
      accuracy = 1
    ),
    scales::percent(
      mean(sweep_results$sd_gain > 0),
      accuracy = 1
    ),
    scales::percent(
      mean(
        sweep_results$delta_mean > 0 &
        sweep_results$sd_gain > 0
      ),
      accuracy = 1
    ),
    paste0(
      "Median Spearman rho = ",
      round(
        median(
          sweep_results$rho_middle_late,
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
        2
      )
    )
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  robustness_summary,
  caption = "Do the main developmental results survive different parameter choices?"
)
```

The figure makes the robustness question more concrete: if most points fall in the upper-right quadrant, the combination of **developmental improvement + increasing between-child differentiation** is not restricted to the single default parameter setting.

The purpose is not to identify the “correct” parameter values. The sampled ranges are theoretical sensitivity ranges. Parameter combinations outside the upper-right quadrant are also informative because they show when the proposed mechanism produces only part of the developmental pattern.

The more detailed parameter-diagnostic plots are kept in the appendix so that they do not interrupt the main argument.

# What have we learned from the minimal model?

The main results can be summarized in six questions.

| Question | What the current model shows |
|---|---|
| **1. What produces developmental improvement?** | EVC-like choice alone is flat; value learning adds modest change; adding practice-related reduction in future effort cost produces much stronger developmental improvement and differentiation. |
| **2. Can initially identical children become different?** | Yes. Different chance engagement and reward experiences generate different $V_t$, $C_t$, and $\pi_t$. Those differences can persist over development, although under a completely shared environment their rank ordering eventually fades. |
| **3. What can make those differences more stable?** | Small persistent differences in how often EF pays off add only modestly to total spread, but they increase rank persistence and imply different long-run mean engagement levels. |
| **4. Can temporary context disrupt engagement?** | Yes. A temporary stressor produces a sharp drop in engagement followed by substantial recovery. Any small residual difference comes indirectly from missed learning and practice opportunities. |
| **5. Is early experience automatically more influential?** | No. When follow-up time is matched, the same reward support given early versus later has very similar effects. The minimal feedback does not by itself create a sensitive period. |
| **6. Are these results tied to one parameter setting?** | The wider replicated parameter sweep tests whether improvement and differentiation occur across a broader region of the model rather than only at the default parameter values. |

The main theoretical story is therefore fairly narrow: repeated engagement changes future learning opportunities, so initially identical children can develop different engagement trajectories. Persistent environmental differences can make those differences more stable. But the model does not automatically produce permanently fixed types or a special advantage of early experience.

# Extension A: Is passive cost stabilization needed?

Yuko previously asked whether a baseline cost level and mean reversion are necessary. We therefore keep this as an **extension**, not part of the core model.

The extension adds

$$
C_{t+1}
=
C_t
+
\eta_C(C_{\mathrm{set}}-C_t)
-
\alpha_C A_t(C_t-C_{\min}).
$$

This is different from the discarded rule $A_t=0\Rightarrow C_{t+1}>C_t$: non-engagement is not itself assigned a penalty. Instead, practice-related cost reductions partly decay unless they are reinforced.

```{r}
#| label: run_cost_stabilization
#| echo: true

df_practice_only <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost",
  N = 1000,
  p_reward_sd = 0,
  seed = 1201
)

df_cost_stabilized <- simulate_population(
  model = "value_cost_stabilized",
  N = 1000,
  p_reward_sd = 0,
  seed = 1201
)

diag_stabilization <- bind_rows(
  df_practice_only,
  df_cost_stabilized
) %>%
  group_by(model_label, step) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_pi = mean(pi),
    sd_pi = sd(pi),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_pi, sd_pi),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      mean_pi = "Population mean propensity",
      sd_pi = "Between-child SD in propensity"
    )
  )

ggplot(
  diag_stabilization,
  aes(step, value, color = model_label)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.0) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_cols) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Passive cost stabilization mainly dampens the feedback",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = NULL,
    color = NULL
  )
```

Under the current parameterization, this extension dampens both mean developmental change and heterogeneity. It is therefore **not needed to produce the core developmental pattern**. We should leave it outside the main model unless a clearer theoretical or empirical reason for passive cost stabilization emerges.

# LEVC and observed performance: when a separate automaticity state becomes necessary

The reparameterization above changes how we should think about the LEVC extension.

For an **engagement-only** model, a separate automaticity state is mathematically redundant with the current practice-dependent cost state. We can write

$$
L_{t+1}
=
L_t+\alpha_C A_t(1-L_t)
$$

and

$$
C_t
=
C_{\min}
+
(C_0-C_{\min})(1-L_t).
$$

Adding both $L_t$ and $C_t$ would therefore add notation without adding a new mechanism.

A distinct automaticity state becomes useful when we want to model **observed EF task performance**. LEVC explicitly treats accuracy as a joint function of automaticity and control intensity. In a developmental extension, we could therefore distinguish:

$$
\text{propensity to engage control}
$$

from

$$
\text{task-specific automaticity}
$$

and let observed performance depend on both:

$$
P(\mathrm{correct})
=
f(\text{control allocated},L_t,\text{task difficulty}).
$$

This allows an important developmental possibility:

$$
L_t\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\text{equal or better performance with less control}.
$$

If we take this route, $C_t$ should no longer silently duplicate automaticity. We would need to decide whether $C$ represents an **inherent subjective cost of control intensity**, while $L$ represents learned task efficiency.

That is a different model and should only be introduced if the target phenomenon is observed EF **performance**, rather than the decision to engage control.

# Overall interpretation

The current model gives a more specific account than the earlier capacity-based version.

First, the strongest developmental change comes from the **practice pathway**: engaging EF provides practice, which gradually lowers the effective effort cost of engaging again. Reward learning also matters, but under the current specification it produces much smaller developmental change on its own.

Second, stable individual differences do not have to be imposed at baseline. Initially identical children can develop different engagement propensities because they experience different engagement and reward sequences by chance. These relative differences can persist over a meaningful developmental period, although they are not permanently fixed when every child continues to experience exactly the same environment.

Third, persistent environmental differences provide one way for later individual differences to remain more stable. If some children consistently experience EF as paying off slightly more often than others, they learn different long-run payoff values and can therefore maintain different mean engagement levels without introducing different EF capacities.

Finally, this experience-dependent feedback does **not** automatically make early experience more powerful than later experience. A genuine early sensitive-period advantage would require an additional developmental assumption rather than following from the current learning and practice dynamics alone.

# What this model does not yet establish

These simulations are theoretical demonstrations. They do not show that:

- generalized EF practice in children actually behaves like task-specific automaticity in LEVC;
- the proposed mapping from practice to effective subjective cost is the true developmental mechanism;
- the current parameter ranges correspond to children or to any particular age range;
- observed EF task scores directly measure engagement propensity;
- reward probability is the only or primary environmental source of individual differences;
- the current dynamics are uniquely supported relative to alternative control-learning models.

The replicated parameter analysis tests sensitivity of the mechanism, not empirical validity. Developmental or experimental data would still be required to constrain the learning rates, practice-related cost-reduction range, environmental inputs, and mapping from latent engagement to observed EF behavior.

# Recommended next steps

1. **Decide what the practice state represents psychologically.** The model only requires a saturating practice-related change in future ease of engagement. If we interpret this as generalized EF automaticity or efficiency, we need to justify transfer across contexts because LEVC itself is task-specific.
2. **Keep the reduced-form $C$ representation for now.** Adding a separate automaticity node would be mathematically redundant unless we also model EF performance.
3. **Check a more canonical LVOC value-learning implementation.** The current delta rule captures the basic experience-learning idea but not LVOC's full feature-based value approximation.
4. **Only add age-dependent plasticity if we explicitly want to explain an early-intervention advantage.** The current feedback does not generate one by itself.
5. **Use candidate longitudinal or experimental data to constrain the mechanisms only after the engagement-versus-performance target is settled.**

# Working interpretation for the paper

A framing consistent with the current model is:

> Existing theories explain how people allocate cognitive control and how experience changes the future value or efficiency of control. We ask what these processes imply when repeated over developmental timescales. In a minimal model, chance differences in experience can generate substantial and moderately persistent differences in EF engagement even when children begin identically. The strongest developmental feedback comes from practice: engaging control creates practice opportunities that can make future engagement easier and therefore more likely. Small persistent differences in how often EF pays off can make later individual differences more stable by producing different long-run mean payoff values. Under a completely shared environment, earlier rank differences eventually lose predictive value. The same feedback does not by itself create an early sensitive-period advantage.

A stronger empirical claim would require evidence that the practice-to-effective-cost mechanism generalizes across the EF contexts relevant to development.

Across the wider replicated sweep:

- `r scales::percent(mean(sweep_results$sd_gain > 0), accuracy = 1)` show greater late than early between-child heterogeneity;
- `r scales::percent(mean(sweep_results$delta_mean > 0 & sweep_results$sd_gain > 0), accuracy = 1)` show **both** patterns;

## How much of the result is Monte Carlo noise?

```{r}
#| label: table_mc_uncertainty
#| echo: true

mc_uncertainty <- tibble(
  outcome = c(
    "Developmental mean change",
    "Heterogeneity change",
    "Middle-to-late rank persistence"
  ),
  median_across_parameter_sets = c(
    median(sweep_results$delta_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(sweep_results$sd_gain, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(sweep_results$rho_middle_late, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  median_within_set_mc_sd = c(
    median(sweep_results$delta_mean_mc_sd, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(sweep_results$sd_gain_mc_sd, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(sweep_results$rho_middle_late_mc_sd, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  mc_uncertainty,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Typical outcome size versus variation across independent simulation replications"
)
```

The replicated design separates **parameter sensitivity** from **simulation noise**. Rank persistence is expected to be noisier than the population mean because it depends on the identities and ordering of individual trajectories.

## How quickly does earlier rank ordering fade?

Result 2 showed that, under a shared environment, children can keep their relative high/low positions for a while but that this ordering eventually becomes less predictive. Here we ask whether that conclusion also holds across the wider parameter sweep.

For every parameter set, we take children's average engagement near the end of the original 900-episode simulation as the **reference ranking**. We then continue the same model much longer and repeatedly ask:

> If a child was relatively high or low around episode 900, how well does that ranking predict where the child stands later?

The correlation is therefore high when the same children tend to remain relatively high or low, and close to zero when the earlier ordering no longer predicts the later ordering.

```{r}
#| label: long_memory_sweep_helpers
#| echo: true

simulate_rank_memory_fast <- function(
  V0,
  C0,
  C_min,
  tau,
  p_reward,
  alpha_V,
  alpha_C,
  reward_mag = default_pars$reward_mag,
  N = 180,
  T0 = 900,
  horizon_multiple = 4,
  centers = seq(1, 4, by = 0.25),
  reference_window = c(0.80, 0.95),
  evaluation_half_width = 0.05,
  seed = 1
) {

  set.seed(seed)

  V <- rep(V0, N)
  C <- rep(C0, N)

  base_intervals <- T0 - 1
  total_T <- round(horizon_multiple * base_intervals) + 1L

  ref_lo <- round(reference_window[1] * base_intervals) + 1L
  ref_hi <- round(reference_window[2] * base_intervals) + 1L

  center_steps <- round(centers * base_intervals) + 1L
  half_width <- max(
    1L,
    round(evaluation_half_width * base_intervals)
  )

  ref_sum <- numeric(N)
  ref_n <- 0L

  score_sums <- matrix(
    0,
    nrow = N,
    ncol = length(centers)
  )
  score_n <- integer(length(centers))

  for (tt in seq_len(total_T)) {

    pi_engage <- plogis((V - C) / tau)

    if (tt >= ref_lo && tt <= ref_hi) {
      ref_sum <- ref_sum + pi_engage
      ref_n <- ref_n + 1L
    }

    active_windows <- which(
      abs(tt - center_steps) <= half_width
    )

    if (length(active_windows) > 0) {
      for (kk in active_windows) {
        score_sums[, kk] <- score_sums[, kk] + pi_engage
        score_n[kk] <- score_n[kk] + 1L
      }
    }

    A <- as.integer(runif(N) < pi_engage)
    reward_success <- as.integer(runif(N) < p_reward)
    reward_observed <- A * reward_success * reward_mag

    V <- V + alpha_V * A * (reward_observed - V)
    C <- C - alpha_C * A * (C - C_min)

    V <- clip(V, lo = 0, hi = reward_mag)
    C <- pmax(C, C_min)
  }

  reference_score <- ref_sum / ref_n

  rank_persistence <- vapply(
    seq_along(centers),
    function(kk) {
      later_score <- score_sums[, kk] / score_n[kk]

      suppressWarnings(
        cor(
          reference_score,
          later_score,
          method = "spearman"
        )
      )
    },
    numeric(1)
  )

  tibble(
    episode = center_steps,
    time_multiple = centers,
    rank_persistence = rank_persistence
  )
}

rank_persistence_metrics <- function(curve_df) {

  curve_df <- curve_df %>%
    arrange(time_multiple)

  get_nearest <- function(target) {
    curve_df$rank_persistence[
      which.min(abs(curve_df$time_multiple - target))
    ]
  }

  tibble(
    rho_2x = get_nearest(2),
    rho_3x = get_nearest(3)
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: run_long_memory_parameter_sweep
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

long_memory_N <- if (quick_sweep) 100 else 180

long_workers <- max(
  1L,
  min(
    n_parameter_sets,
    parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE) - 1L
  )
)

if (is.na(long_workers) || long_workers < 1L) {
  long_workers <- 1L
}

long_memory_list <- parallel_lapply(
  seq_len(n_parameter_sets),

  function(j) {

    pars_j <- sweep_pars[j, ]

    curve_j <- simulate_rank_memory_fast(
      V0 = pars_j$V0,
      C0 = pars_j$C0,
      C_min = pars_j$C_min,
      tau = pars_j$tau,
      p_reward = pars_j$p_reward,
      alpha_V = pars_j$alpha_V,
      alpha_C = pars_j$alpha_C,
      N = long_memory_N,
      T0 = sweep_T,
      seed = 300000 + j
    )

    curve_j %>%
      mutate(set_id = pars_j$set_id)
  },

  workers = long_workers
)

long_memory_curves <- bind_rows(
  long_memory_list
)

long_memory_metrics_df <- long_memory_curves %>%
  group_by(set_id) %>%
  group_modify(
    ~ rank_persistence_metrics(.x)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(
    sweep_pars,
    by = "set_id"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig_long_memory_across_parameters
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center

long_memory_band <- long_memory_curves %>%
  group_by(episode, time_multiple) %>%
  summarize(
    q10 = quantile(rank_persistence, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(rank_persistence, na.rm = TRUE),
    q90 = quantile(rank_persistence, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  long_memory_band,
  aes(episode, median)
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = q10, ymax = q90),
    alpha = 0.18
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = 1.0
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(sweep_T, 4 * sweep_T),
    ylim = c(-0.10, 1)
  ) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Earlier rank ordering becomes less predictive over time",
    subtitle = "Black line = median across parameter sets; band = 10th-90th percentile",
    x = "Developmental episode t",
    y = "Correlation with the earlier ranking"
  )
```

Across the parameter sweep, the same general pattern appears: earlier rank ordering becomes progressively less predictive as the simulation continues. The wide band shows that **the speed of this decline differs substantially across parameter settings**.

So the useful conclusion is not that every simulation loses rank ordering at exactly the same time. It is that under a shared environment, earlier high/low positions generally fade, while the model parameters affect **how quickly** they fade.

### Which parameters are most clearly related to faster fading?

Rather than show a large table of every parameter-outcome correlation, we focus on the two clearest associations from the sweep: the value-learning rate $\alpha_V$ and decision temperature $\tau$.

To keep the outcome easy to interpret, the y-axis below is simply the correlation between children's ranking near the end of the original simulation and their ranking around **three times that simulation length** (approximately episode `r 3 * sweep_T`).

```{r}
#| label: fig_long_memory_key_parameters
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-align: center
#| message: false

rho_alphaV_3x <- cor(
  long_memory_metrics_df$alpha_V,
  long_memory_metrics_df$rho_3x,
  method = "spearman",
  use = "complete.obs"
)

rho_tau_3x <- cor(
  long_memory_metrics_df$tau,
  long_memory_metrics_df$rho_3x,
  method = "spearman",
  use = "complete.obs"
)

long_memory_key <- bind_rows(
  long_memory_metrics_df %>%
    transmute(
      parameter = "Value-learning rate α_V",
      parameter_value = alpha_V,
      rank_correlation_3x = rho_3x
    ),
  long_memory_metrics_df %>%
    transmute(
      parameter = "Decision temperature τ",
      parameter_value = tau,
      rank_correlation_3x = rho_3x
    )
)

ggplot(
  long_memory_key,
  aes(parameter_value, rank_correlation_3x)
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.35,
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ parameter,
    scales = "free_x"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(-0.15, 0.85)
  ) +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Faster value updating and higher decision temperature are linked to faster loss of rank ordering",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Spearman associations with rank persistence at ~3× the original horizon: ",
      "α_V = ",
      round(rho_alphaV_3x, 2),
      "; τ = ",
      round(rho_tau_3x, 2)
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Correlation with earlier ranking at ~3× horizon"
  )
```

In this model, larger $\alpha_V$ means that recent reward experience updates $V_t$ more quickly, so earlier value histories are overwritten faster. Larger $\tau$ makes engagement less sensitive to differences in $V_t-C_t$, so earlier relative differences in learned value and cost are expressed less strongly in behavior.

These are **descriptive model sensitivities**, not estimates of developmental effects in children. The main reason to retain them is that they show why some parameter settings preserve individual ordering longer than others.

## Direct check of the practice mechanism

Because the theoretical account depends on practice making later engagement easier, it is useful to look directly at the two practice-related parameters. The figure below asks a simple question:

- When practice reduces future effort cost **faster** ($\alpha_C$), do we see more developmental change?
- When there is **more room** for practice to reduce future effort cost ($C_0 - C_{\min}$), do we see more developmental change?

The **bottom row** is the main part to look at: it shows how these two practice parameters relate to the increase in **mean EF engagement** from early to late development. The **top row** shows their relation to the increase in between-child spread.



Because the theoretical result depends on practice changing future ease of control, it is useful to visualize that dependency directly.

```{r}
#| label: fig_practice_sensitivity
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-align: center
#| message: false

practice_sensitivity <- bind_rows(
  sweep_results %>%
    transmute(
      parameter = "Practice learning rate α_C",
      parameter_value = alpha_C,
      developmental_change = delta_mean,
      heterogeneity_change = sd_gain
    ),
  sweep_results %>%
    transmute(
      parameter = "Amount of practice-related cost reduction available",
      parameter_value = practice_range,
      developmental_change = delta_mean,
      heterogeneity_change = sd_gain
    )
) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(developmental_change, heterogeneity_change),
    names_to = "outcome",
    values_to = "outcome_value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    outcome = recode(
      outcome,
      developmental_change = "Late - early mean propensity",
      heterogeneity_change = "Late - early between-child SD"
    )
  )

practice_sensitivity <- practice_sensitivity %>%
  mutate(
    panel = paste(
      outcome,
      parameter,
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )

ggplot(
  practice_sensitivity,
  aes(parameter_value, outcome_value)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free") +
  theme_result() +
  labs(
    title = "Practice parameters mainly shape average developmental improvement",
    subtitle = "Bottom row is the key result: stronger practice effects are associated with larger increases in mean engagement",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  )
```

The clearest pattern is in the **bottom row**: developmental improvement tends to be larger when practice reduces future effort cost more quickly ($\alpha_C$) and when more practice-related cost reduction is available ($C_0 - C_{\min}$). In other words, stronger practice effects are associated with larger increases in mean EF engagement.

The **top row** is less clean. The same practice parameters show a weaker and noisier relation to the increase in between-child spread. So the safest interpretation is that these practice parameters primarily control **how much the population improves on average**, while their association with differentiation is more variable.

This remains a diagnostic view of the model rather than an empirical claim about the true values of these parameters in children.
